sections.h2: Which closing costs hit a Florida seller?
sections.html:
On the statute side, the big items are the stamp tax on the deed, the clerk's recording charges, title work and the seller's slice of the year's property tax. Commissions, repair credits and association fees come from the contract, not from state law. Florida contracts leave much of this open, so the signed paper decides who pays each line.

This page covers the charges that a Florida statute or the Department of Revenue puts in writing. Ask your title agent or closing attorney to explain any other line on the settlement statement before closing day.

sections.h2: What does the deed stamp tax come to?
sections.html:
The statutory rate is seventy cents for every $100 of consideration, counting any part of a hundred, in every county but Miami-Dade. Section 201.02 states it, and the Department of Revenue repeats it. Consideration is a wide term: cash, a debt you are released from, and any mortgage or encumbrance on the parcel all count, whether or not the buyer assumes the loan.

Miami-Dade prints sixty cents per $100 plus a 45 cent surtax per $100. The surtax is skipped when the paper transfers only a single-family dwelling, so the clerk in that county can tell you which version fits your deed.

Payment goes to the county clerk at recording. A deed is taxable recorded or not, and a taxable paper that never gets recorded is paid to the Department itself. After a foreclosure sale, the certificate of title is taxed on the highest and best bid, per section 201.02(9).

sections.h2: Who is responsible for paying doc stamps?
sections.html:
Your contract names the payer, yet the state treats everyone on the document as liable. The Department says liability stays with all parties whichever one agreed to pay, and a non-exempt party covers the tax when another party is exempt. No statute assigns the deed tax to a particular side.

If you agreed to pay, expect the title agent to subtract the tax from your proceeds at the table. The Department lists these exemptions and exclusions:

  • A spousal homestead deed where a mortgage is the only consideration.
  • A divorce deed for the marital home.
  • A deed by a personal representative acting under a probated will, which the Department lists as not taxable.

sections.h2: How does the buyer's loan change the picture?
sections.html:
Mortgages and notes are taxed separately from the deed. The Department prints 35 cents on each $100 secured, with the note tax limited to $2,450 and no limit on mortgages. These charges follow the buyer's financing, so an all-cash buyer has none of them.

On your side, a lender holding your own mortgage will want payoff in full at closing. Order a written payoff statement a few days ahead, since interest accrues daily and the figure moves.

sections.h2: How much does the clerk charge to record a deed?
sections.html:
Under section 28.24, an instrument of ordinary size costs $5.00 for the first page and $4.00 for every added page, with a $1.00 charge for each name past the fourth. A trust fund charge of $1.00 on page one and 50 cents on later pages sits on top, plus a $4 per page technology charge.

That adds up to far less than the stamp tax. A long deed with many grantors costs more than a short one, so have the closing agent quote the recording total before closing.

sections.h2: Does the seller pay for title insurance?
sections.html:
Whoever pays, the premium schedule comes from state rule. Florida's rule on title insurance rates cites sections 627.782 and 627.7825 as its authority. Your contract names the party who buys the owner's policy, so read its title paragraph.

Section 627.7841 gives one protection worth knowing. If the insurer's own officers, employees or agents disburse your closing funds, the insurer must cover defects recorded after the commitment date and before the deed is recorded, except those the insured knows about. That is a reason to close through a title agent who handles the money.

sections.h2: What happens with property taxes and listing disclosures?
sections.html:
Tax bills arrive in November and carry an early-payment discount that steps down month by month until February. Unpaid taxes turn delinquent on April 1. The closing agent normally splits the annual bill between you and the buyer according to the contract, and the tax collector can give you the current amount.

Residential buyers must get a property tax disclosure at or before signing under section 689.261. It warns that the seller's present bill is a poor guide, because a sale or new improvements triggers reassessment. The statute adds that from February 1, 2027, listing materials may not show the current owner's tax amount, so ask your agent how your listing will read.

faqs.q: Who ends up paying the deed stamps?
faqs.a: Whoever your contract says, though the state holds every party liable. The Department of Revenue says liability stays with all parties on the document. Read the closing cost paragraph for the agreed payer.

faqs.q: Will a cash buyer owe the mortgage tax?
faqs.a: No. That tax applies to mortgages and notes at 35 cents per $100 secured, and a cash purchase creates neither. Only the deed tax and recording charges remain.
Yes. The Department prints 60 cents per $100 plus a 45 cent surtax, and the surtax is not due on a paper transferring only a single-family dwelling.

faqs.q: What is the recording charge for a deed?
faqs.a: Section 28.24 sets $5.00 for page one and $4.00 per added page, with a trust fund charge, a $4 per page technology charge and $1.00 per name past four.

faqs.q: When do property tax bills come and go delinquent?
faqs.a: Bills are mailed in November, and unpaid ones become delinquent on April 1. Your closing agent prorates the year between you and the buyer.
